analogy: A variable is a name tag stuck on a value, so you can find the value by its name.
breaks: A tag sits on one value at a time; it never holds two values at once.
source: Hermans et al. 2018: labels beat boxes for the 'holds two values' mistake

analogy: Assigning moves the name tag onto a new value; the old value is no longer under that name.
mapping: the old value is dropped from the name
breaks: In maths '=' means 'is equal'; in code it means 'now points to', so x = x + 1 is fine in code.

analogy: Data types are different containers: a jar for liquids, a box for objects. Each holds one kind of thing well.
mapping: pouring soup into a paper bag fails
breaks: Some languages convert types for you automatically, which real jars never do.

analogy: An array is an egg tray: a row of numbered cups, one item per cup, found by position.
breaks: Many lists can grow and shrink; a real tray has a fixed number of cups.

analogy: Indexes start at 0 like floors in many buildings: the ground floor is 0, the next is floor 1.
breaks: Some buildings call the ground floor 1, just as some languages (Lua, R) start lists at 1.

analogy: A dictionary is a chest of labelled drawers: you open a drawer by its label, not by counting.
mapping: no two drawers share a label
breaks: Real drawers sit in an order; many dictionaries don't promise any order.

analogy: A function is a recipe card: the same steps every time, used whenever you need that dish.
breaks: A recipe can be followed loosely; a function does exactly the same steps every time.

analogy: A function is a vending machine: put in a coin and a choice, get one snack out.
breaks: Some functions do things besides returning a result, like printing or saving a file.

analogy: A for loop is running laps with a counter: run, add one, stop at the target.
mapping: one pass through the loop body
breaks: A runner gets tired; a loop runs each pass exactly the same way.

analogy: A while loop is stirring a sauce until it's thick: check, stir, check again.
mapping: loop ends when the condition is false
breaks: If the sauce never thickens you'd notice; a program can loop forever unless the condition can change.

analogy: An if-statement is a fork in the road: one sign decides which path you take.
breaks: You can walk back on a road; a program doesn't go back unless told to.

analogy: Conditions work like a traffic light: red means stop, green means go, checked in a fixed order.
breaks: A traffic light shows one colour; several conditions can be true at once, and the first one wins.

analogy: A boolean is a light switch: only on (true) or off (false).
breaks: Some values act like true or false without being booleans (like 0 or an empty list).

analogy: Recursion is opening nesting dolls: open one, find a smaller one, until the smallest that doesn't open.
breaks: The dolls already exist; recursion makes each smaller call as it goes, and needs a base case to stop.

analogy: The call stack is a stack of plates: each new call goes on top and must finish before the one under it.
breaks: You can grab a plate from the middle; a program only works on the top call.

analogy: A stack is a pile of plates: the last plate you put on is the first you take off.
breaks: None worth noting for beginners: stacks really behave like this.

analogy: A queue is a line at a bus stop: first to arrive, first to get on.
breaks: People sometimes cut in line; a plain queue never lets anyone skip (a priority queue does).

analogy: A linked list is a treasure hunt: each clue tells you where the next clue is hidden.
mapping: the pointer to the next node
the node that points to nothing
breaks: To reach clue 10 you must follow 1 to 9 first; you can't jump there like in an array.

analogy: A tree is like folders on a computer: one top folder, folders inside folders, files at the ends.
breaks: A real tree grows up from the root; computer trees are drawn with the root at the top.

analogy: A graph is a map of towns and roads: towns are nodes, roads are edges.
breaks: Roads go both ways; some graph edges are one-way.

analogy: Sorting is arranging books on a shelf by height, swapping two at a time until all are in order.
breaks: You see the whole shelf at once; a computer can only compare two items at a time.

analogy: Binary search is finding a word in a dictionary: open the middle, keep the half it must be in, repeat.
breaks: It only works when the list is already sorted, like a dictionary is.

analogy: Big O asks how the work grows: finding a book in a messy pile takes longer per book added than on a sorted shelf.
breaks: Big O ignores small fixed costs, so a 'slower' method can win on tiny lists.

analogy: A class is a cookie cutter; objects are the cookies. Same shape, each cookie its own.
breaks: A cookie can't do anything; objects also carry actions (methods).

analogy: A class is a house blueprint; each object is a real house built from it.
breaks: Changing a blueprint doesn't change built houses; in some languages changing a class affects existing objects.

analogy: Inheritance is family traits: a child gets the parent's features and can add its own.
breaks: Real children mix two parents; most classes inherit from one, and they inherit exactly.

analogy: Encapsulation is a TV remote: you press buttons and never touch the wiring inside.
breaks: Programmers can usually still look inside if they really want to.

analogy: An API is a restaurant waiter: you order from the menu, the waiter talks to the kitchen and brings back your food.
breaks: A waiter can guess what you meant; an API needs the request in exactly the right format.

analogy: A library is a toolbox of ready-made tools: you import it instead of making a hammer yourself.
breaks: A tool doesn't change; libraries get new versions that can break your code.

analogy: A compiler translates a whole book before anyone reads it; an interpreter translates live, sentence by sentence.
breaks: Many real languages mix both, compiling to an in-between form and interpreting that.

analogy: Debugging is detective work: collect clues, make a guess, test it, rule suspects out.
breaks: A detective's suspect stays put; a bug can move when you add prints or change timing.

analogy: A commit is a save point in a game: you can always go back to it.
breaks: Game saves overwrite; git keeps every save point in history.

analogy: A branch is a separate draft of an essay; merging copies the good changes back into the main essay.
mapping: two drafts changed the same sentence
breaks: Branches are cheap pointers, not full copies of every file.

analogy: RAM is your desk: small but quick to reach. Storage is the drawers: big, slower, keeps things when you leave.
mapping: RAM empties when power is off
breaks: A desk doesn't forget; RAM loses everything when the computer turns off.

analogy: A cache is milk in your fridge: you keep a copy close so you don't walk to the market every time.
breaks: Milk tells you when it's off; stale cached data looks fresh unless you check.

analogy: A CPU is a few expert chefs; a GPU is hundreds of helpers who each chop one vegetable at the same time.
mapping: CPU core: fast at any task
GPU cores: simple tasks in parallel
breaks: Kitchen helpers can talk freely; GPU cores share work in strict groups.

analogy: Threads are two cooks in one kitchen: faster together, but they can grab the same pot.
breaks: Cooks can see each other; threads can't, so they need explicit locks.

analogy: Deadlock is two cars on a one-lane bridge, each waiting for the other to back up.
breaks: Drivers can talk and agree; programs need a rule decided in advance to avoid it.

analogy: A database is a library catalogue: neat cards you can search, sort and update quickly.
breaks: A catalogue is read by people; databases also stop two people changing the same card at once.

analogy: A database index is the index at the back of a book: jump to the page instead of reading every page.
breaks: A book index never changes; a database index must be updated on every write, which costs time.

analogy: An IP address is a house address for a device, so messages know where to go.
breaks: A house keeps its address; many devices get a new IP address when they reconnect.

analogy: DNS is your phone's contact list: you tap a name and it finds the number.
breaks: Your contact list lives on your phone; DNS answers come from servers around the world.

analogy: Data is sent like a puzzle posted in pieces: each piece travels on its own and is put back together at the end.
breaks: Lost puzzle pieces are gone; lost packets are sent again automatically.

analogy: HTTP is exchanging letters: your browser writes 'please send this page', the server writes back with it.
breaks: Letters take days; HTTP replies take milliseconds, and the server forgets you after each letter.

analogy: A client is a customer and a server is the kitchen: customers ask, the kitchen prepares and sends.
breaks: One kitchen serves a few tables; one server can serve millions of clients at once.

analogy: The cloud is renting computers instead of buying them, like renting a car only on the days you need one.
breaks: The cloud isn't in the sky: it's real computers in big buildings.

analogy: Public-key encryption is an open padlock you hand out: anyone can snap it shut on a box, only you have the key.
breaks: Real padlocks can be cut; good encryption would take impossibly long to break.

analogy: A hash is a fingerprint of data: small, unique-looking, and you can't rebuild the person from it.
breaks: Two different inputs can share a hash (a collision), though good hashes make it very rare.

analogy: A firewall is a security guard at the gate, checking who comes in and out against a list.
breaks: A guard can spot something odd; a firewall only follows its rules.

analogy: Bandwidth is how wide the pipe is; latency is how long the pipe is. Wide pipes move more, short pipes arrive sooner.
breaks: Water flows smoothly; network data comes in packets that can queue up.

analogy: Binary is a row of light switches: each is on (1) or off (0), and each switch counts double the one to its right.
breaks: None big: the counting really works like this.

analogy: Training a model is studying with flashcards: guess, check the answer, adjust, repeat thousands of times.
breaks: You understand why; a model only adjusts numbers and can't explain itself.

analogy: Overfitting is memorising last year's exam answers: perfect on old papers, lost on new questions.
breaks: A student knows they memorised; a model can't tell, so we test it on unseen data.

analogy: Gradient descent is walking down a hill in fog: feel which way is steepest, take a step, repeat.
breaks: You might stop in a small dip, not the deepest valley (a local minimum).

analogy: A neural network is rows of voters: each listens to the row before, weighs their votes, and passes on its own.
mapping: how much a voter trusts a friend
breaks: Real brain cells work very differently; the name is only a loose inspiration.

analogy: Async code is a restaurant buzzer: you order, sit down and chat, and it buzzes when your food is ready.
breaks: You hear one buzz; async code can have many tasks finishing in any order.

analogy: Garbage collection is café staff clearing cups nobody is using any more.
breaks: Staff ask before taking a cup; the collector decides only by whether anything still points to it.

analogy: A fraction is slices of a pizza: the bottom says how many equal slices, the top says how many you have.
breaks: Pizza slices are rarely equal; fractions always mean exactly equal parts.

analogy: Negative numbers are floors below ground in a lift: 0 is ground, -2 is two floors down.
breaks: Lifts don't multiply; why minus times minus is plus needs a different picture.

analogy: An equation is a balanced scale: whatever you do to one side, do to the other so it stays level.
mapping: adding the same weight to both
breaks: A scale can't hold negative weights; equations can.

analogy: In algebra, x is a closed box with a number inside: the equation's clues tell you what's in it.
breaks: In maths x stands for one fixed number; in code a variable can change (that's why code uses name tags).

analogy: A function is a machine: put a number in, it follows one rule, one number comes out.
breaks: A machine could jam or give different results; a function always gives the same output for the same input.

analogy: Slope is how steep a hill is: how far up you go for each step forward.
breaks: A hill's steepness changes as you walk; a straight line's slope never does.

analogy: A derivative is a speedometer: it shows how fast something is changing at this exact moment.
breaks: A speedometer measures one thing; a derivative works for any changing quantity, even negative changes.

analogy: An integral is how much water a tank holds after a tap ran at changing speeds: add up every little bit.
breaks: A tank can't hold negative water; an integral can be negative when the function is below zero.

analogy: A limit is walking half the way to a wall, then half again, forever: you get as close as you like to the wall.
breaks: Real legs stop eventually; in maths the steps go on forever.

analogy: Probability is pulling a marble from a bag without looking: more red marbles, more chance of red.
breaks: It assumes every marble is equally likely to be picked, which real situations don't always give you.

analogy: Exponential growth is a snowball rolling downhill: the bigger it gets, the faster it grows.
breaks: A real snowball runs out of hill; pure exponential growth never slows.

analogy: A logarithm counts how many times you double (or multiply) to reach a number: log2 of 8 is 3 doublings.
breaks: Logs also exist for numbers that aren't a whole number of doublings, like log2 of 10.

analogy: A vector is a treasure-map instruction: 'walk 3 steps east and 4 north'. Size and direction together.
breaks: On a map the start point matters; a vector is the same wherever it starts.

analogy: A proof is a detective's case: each step follows from facts already accepted, until the conclusion is certain.
breaks: A detective can be 'nearly sure'; a proof must leave no room for doubt.

analogy: A percentage is 'out of 100': 25% of a pile of 100 coins is 25 coins.
breaks: The whole isn't always 100 things; 25% of 40 coins is 10.

analogy: Voltage is water pressure in a pipe: the push that makes the water (charge) flow.
breaks: Water leaks out of a cut pipe; electricity needs a complete loop to flow at all.

analogy: Current is how much water flows past a point each second.
breaks: Electrons drift slowly; the push travels along the wire almost instantly.

analogy: Resistance is a narrow part of the pipe: same pressure, less water gets through.
mapping: more pressure for the same flow
breaks: A resistor gets hot; the water picture doesn't show where the energy goes.

analogy: Inertia is a full shopping cart: hard to start moving, and hard to stop once it rolls.
breaks: A real cart slows by itself because of friction; with no friction it would roll forever.

analogy: Momentum is why a moving bus is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed.
breaks: Momentum also has a direction; a bus going left and one going right can cancel out.

analogy: Energy is like money moving between jars: it changes jar (motion, height, heat) but the total stays the same.
breaks: You can see coins; energy 'lost' to heat is still there, just spread out and hard to use.

analogy: A heavy ball on a trampoline makes a dip; smaller balls roll towards it, like planets curving around the Sun.
breaks: The trampoline uses Earth's gravity to make the dip, which is the very thing it tries to explain.

analogy: A wave is a stadium wave: each person only stands and sits, yet the wave travels round the stadium.
breaks: Light needs no people at all: it travels through empty space.

analogy: Heat moves from hot to cold like a crowd spreading from a packed room into an empty one.
breaks: People choose where to go; heat spreads only because of random jiggling of particles.

analogy: Electron shells are rows of seats around a stage: the front row fills first and holds the fewest.
breaks: Electrons aren't in fixed seats; they're spread out in clouds of probability.

analogy: A covalent bond is two friends holding hands: each shares a hand, and the sharing keeps them together.
breaks: Friends hold hands equally; some atoms pull shared electrons harder (polar bonds).

analogy: A catalyst is a matchmaker: it brings the right partners together faster and walks away unchanged.
breaks: A matchmaker can change who meets; a catalyst never changes which products form.

analogy: Dynamic equilibrium is two escalators, up and down, carrying people at the same rate: both floors stay equally busy.
mapping: crowd on each floor stays the same
breaks: People choose to ride; molecules react randomly, and the amounts on each side needn't be equal.

analogy: Concentration is how sweet your tea is: more sugar in the same cup, or the same sugar in less tea, is sweeter.
breaks: Sugar stops dissolving at some point; that limit (saturation) is its own idea.

analogy: A cell is a busy factory: an office with the plans, power stations, assembly lines and a gate.
breaks: Factory workers decide things; a cell's parts just follow chemistry, with no boss.

analogy: Mitochondria are the cell's power stations: they turn food into a form of energy the cell can spend.
breaks: Power stations make electricity; mitochondria make ATP, a chemical 'energy coin'.

analogy: DNA is a cookbook: each gene is one recipe for making one protein.
breaks: A cookbook is read front to back; cells switch recipes on and off as needed.

analogy: An enzyme is a lock and its substrate is the key: only the right shape fits the active site.
breaks: Real active sites bend a little to fit (induced fit), unlike a rigid lock.

analogy: The immune system is security staff who check ID cards and remember faces of past troublemakers.
breaks: Guards are trained once; the immune system keeps making new kinds of 'guards' by chance.

analogy: Neurons pass signals like a relay race: each runner carries the message and hands it on across a small gap.
breaks: Runners slow down when tired; nerve signals stay the same strength along the way.

analogy: Evolution is copying a recipe by hand for generations: small typos creep in, and versions that cook better get copied more.
breaks: Nobody chooses the 'better' recipe on purpose; the environment does it without any plan.

analogy: The heart is two pumps side by side: one sends blood to the lungs, the other to the whole body.
breaks: A pump runs on electricity; the heart's muscle sets its own beat.

analogy: Concert tickets: few tickets and many fans push the price up; empty seats push it down.
breaks: Some prices are fixed by law or habit and don't move with demand.

analogy: Inflation is when the same coins buy less at the market each year.
breaks: Wages can rise too, so people aren't always poorer; it depends on what rises faster.

analogy: Compound interest is a snowball: interest is added, then you earn interest on that interest too.
breaks: It works the same way on debts, and there it grows against you.

analogy: Opportunity cost is the road you didn't take: choosing one path means giving up the other.
breaks: The cost is only the best option you gave up, not every option.

analogy: A budget is splitting your money into jars before spending: food, travel, savings.
breaks: Real costs surprise you; good budgets keep one jar for surprises.

analogy: Competition is a street of food stalls: if one charges too much, customers walk to the next stall.
mapping: only one stall on the street
breaks: Switching isn't always easy online or in big markets, so competition can be weaker than it looks.

analogy: Don't put all your eggs in one basket: if it drops, you lose them all.
breaks: If everything falls together (a market crash), many baskets still break at once.

analogy: Memory is a plant: water it a little over many days and it grows strong; one flood on one day doesn't help much.
breaks: Plants need water on a fixed schedule; reviews should get further apart as you remember better.

analogy: Pulling an answer from memory is lifting a weight: the effort is what makes it stronger. Rereading is watching someone else lift.
breaks: Muscles need rest days; memory benefits from short, frequent practice instead.

analogy: Working memory is a small desk: only a few things fit at once, so put one idea down before picking up the next.
breaks: A desk can be cleared on purpose; working memory fades on its own within seconds.

analogy: Learning something new is juggling: each new idea is another ball, and too many at once means you drop them all.
mapping: an idea you know well, nearly free to juggle
breaks: Some ideas group into one chunk, which is like taping two balls together.

analogy: A habit is a path through grass: walk it every day and it becomes the easy way.
breaks: Paths grow back slowly; old habits can return fast under stress.

analogy: Attention is a torch in a dark room: whatever it points at is clear, everything else stays dim.
breaks: A torch is steady; attention drifts by itself, which is normal, not a failure.
